column2: That king, a yogi, drank the watery force of him and by yoga quenched the fire with water.
Having killed that huge water-Rakshasa by force, the king, his work done, showed him (the dead Dhundhu) to Uttanka.
Uttanka granted a boon to that great-souled king: he gave him imperishable wealth, unconquerable by enemies,
constant delight in dharma, imperishable residence in heaven, and imperishable worlds in heaven for the sons who were slain by the Rakshasa.
Three sons of his remained: Dridhashva is called the eldest; Chandrashva and Kapilashva were the younger boys.
Of Dridhashva, son of Dhundhumara, Haryashva is remembered as son; Haryashva's son was Nikumbha, always devoted to Kshatriya dharma.
Nikumbha's son was Samhatashva, skilled in battle; Akrishashva and Krishashva were Samhatashva's sons, Brahmins.
His daughter Drishadvati, from the Himalaya (family), esteemed by the good, was famed in the three worlds; her son was Prasenajit.
Prasenajit obtained a devoted wife named Gauri; cursed by her husband, she became the river Bahuda.
His great son was King Yuvanashva; Yuvanashva's son was Mandhata, conqueror of the three worlds.
His wife, the daughter of Shashabindu from the Chaitraratha line, was the virtuous Bindumati, unequalled on earth in beauty,
devoted to her husband and the eldest of ten thousand brothers. On her Mandhata begot two sons, Brahmins:
Purukutsa, a knower of dharma, and King Muchukunda. Purukutsa's son was the king Trasadasyu,
born of Narmada; his son was Sambhuta, and Sambhuta's heir was Tridhanva, crusher of foes.
King Tridhanva's son was the learned lord Trayyaruna; his son was a very mighty boy named Satyavrata.
The very evil-minded one obstructed the marriage mantras, by which a wife who had been wedded was carried off from another.
From childishness, lust, delusion, rashness and fickleness, tormented by desire he abducted the daughter of some city-dweller.
With suspicion of unrighteousness, Trayyaruna cast him off, angrily saying "Get out!" many times.
Abandoned, he said repeatedly to his father, "Where shall I go?" And his father said to him, "Live with the dog-cookers (Shvapakas).
I do not need a son from such a son, stain of the family." Thus told, he left the city at his father's word.
The revered sage Vasishtha did not stop him. Satyavrata, Brahmins, lived near the dwellings of the Shvapakas,
the hero abandoned by his father; his father also went to the forest. Then in that country Indra did not rain
for twelve years, Brahmins, because of that unrighteousness. In that country the wife of the great ascetic Vishvamitra, left behind,
while he performed vast austerity at the sea's end, tied her middle natural son by the neck
and sold him for a hundred cows to feed the rest. Seeing him bound by the neck for sale, the king's son, righteous-souled,
released the great sage's son, Brahmins; the mighty-armed Satyavrata also supported him,
to please Vishvamitra and out of compassion. He became known as Galava, because he had been bound by the neck, a great ascetic; the great sage Kaushika the wise was freed by that hero.
She, having made a pyre for her husband in the forest, climbed onto it; Aurva the Bhargava, out of compassion, stopped her, Brahmins.
In his hermitage that child, together with the poison (gara) given to her, was born, the mighty-armed king named Sagara.
Aurva performed the birth rites and the rest for the great-souled boy, taught him the Vedas and the sciences, then gave him the weapon,
the fire-weapon, fortunate ones, unbearable even to the immortals. With the power of that weapon and his strength, in battle
he quickly slew the Haihayas, angry like Rudra among beasts, and won fame in the worlds, the best of the famous.
Then the king resolved to destroy completely the Shakas, Yavanas, Kambojas, Paradas and Pahlavas.
Being slain by the great-souled hero Sagara, they went to the wise Vasishtha for refuge and bowed down.
Vasishtha, of great radiance, seeing them, by an agreement restrained Sagara, giving them assurance of safety.
Sagara, hearing his teacher's word and mindful of his own vow, destroyed their dharma and made other dress for them.
He shaved half the heads of the Shakas and let them go; the Yavanas had their whole heads shaved, and likewise the Kambojas.
The Paradas were made loose-haired, the Pahlavas beard-wearing; by that great-souled king they were deprived of Vedic study and the vashat call.
The Shakas, Yavanas, Kambojas and Paradas, best of Brahmins, the Konisarpas, Mahishakas, Darvas, Cholas and Keralas —
all of these, Brahmins, were Kshatriyas, whose dharma was removed by the great-souled king Sagara at Vasishtha's word.
That king, victorious through dharma, having conquered this earth, consecrated for the horse-sacrifice, let a horse roam.
As he let it roam, that horse in the south-eastern sea near the shore was stolen and led into the earth.
The king had that place dug by his sons. While the great ocean was being dug, they came upon
that primal being, God Hari, Krishna, the Prajapati Vishnu, then asleep in the form of Kapila.
By the brilliance arising from his eyes as he awoke, all were burnt, best of sages, except four who remained:
Barhiketu, Suketu, King Dharmaratha, and Shura Panchanada: these kings were the continuers of his line.
The revered Hari-Narayana gave him a boon: an imperishable line of Ikshvaku and unfailing fame,
a son — Samudra (the Ocean) — and an imperishable abode in heaven. The Ocean took an arghya and bowed to that king.
By that deed he obtained the name Sagara's (ocean's) own; and he got that sacrificial horse back from the ocean.
That great ascetic performed a hundred horse-sacrifices, and we have heard that he had sixty thousand sons.
How were the heroic sons of Sagara born, greatly mighty and valiant, sixty thousand, by what procedure, best one?
Sagara had two wives, whose sins were burned away by austerity: the elder was a daughter of the Vidarbha king, named Keshini,
and the younger, great and exceedingly righteous, was a daughter of Arishtanemi, unequalled on earth in beauty.
Aurva gave them a boon; understand that, best of Brahmins: "One of the fair-hipped women may take sixty thousand sons,
and the other one son to continue the line; let each choose as she wishes." Thereupon one took sons numbering sixty thousand;
the other chose one son to carry the line. The sage said "So be it." Then a king named Panchajana, of great radiance, came to be.
The other bore a gourd full of seeds, so the tradition says; in it were sixty thousand embryos, the size of sesame seeds.
In due time they came to be and grew happily. Then he placed those embryos in pots full of ghee.
The king gave one nurse for each, as many for their nourishment; then after ten months they rose up in order.
Those boys, in due time, increasing Sagara's joy, thus became his sixty thousand sons, Brahmins,
born from the middle of the gourd-womb of the king of the earth. Of those great-souled ones who had entered Narayana's brilliance,
one, Panchajana, became king. Panchajana's son was the valiant Anshuman.
His son Dilipa was famed as Khatvanga, who, coming from heaven here and gaining a moment of life,
won the three worlds by intellect and truth, sinless one. Dilipa's heir was the great king Bhagiratha,
the lord who brought down the Ganga, best of rivers, led her to the ocean and made her his daughter;
therefore the Ganga is called Bhagirathi by those versed in genealogies. Bhagiratha's son was the king famed as Shruta.
Nabhaga was Shruta's very righteous son; Ambarisha, the son of Nabhaga, was the father of Sindhudvipa.
Sindhudvipa's valiant heir was Ayutajit; Ayutajit's son was Rituparna of great fame,
the king, knower of the secret of dice, friend of Nala, mighty. Rituparna's son was the greatly famed Artaparni.
His son was Sudasa, a king, friend of Indra; Sudasa's son is called the king Saudasa.
The famed Kalmashapada, also Mitrasaha, was king; Kalmashapada's son was known as Sarvakarma.
Anaranya was the famed son of Sarvakarma; Anaranya's son was Nighna, and Nighna had two sons:
Anamitra and Raghu, the two best of royal bulls. Anamitra's son, a king, was the learned Duliduha.
His son was Dilipa, great-grandfather of Rama. Dilipa's son was named Raghu, long-armed.
The great king in Ayodhya who was mighty of old, Aja the Raghava, was born; and Dasharatha was born of Aja.
From Dasharatha was born Rama, righteous-souled and greatly famed. Rama's son was born, named Kusha.
Atithi was born of Kusha, righteous-souled and greatly famed. Atithi's son was the valiant Nishadha.
Nishadha's son was Nala, Nala's son Nabha; Nabha's son is remembered as Pundarika, then Kshemadhanva.
Kshemadhanva's son was the mighty Devanika; Devanika's son the lord Ahinagu.
Ahinagu's heir was a king named Sudhanva; Sudhanva's son was then born, King Shala.
The righteous-souled Ukya was the son of Shala; Vajranabha was his son, and his (son) was the great-souled Nala.
Two Nalas alone are famed in the Purana, best of sages; one a son of Virasena, and the other who upheld the Ikshvaku family.
Those born in the Ikshvaku line have been chiefly named. These are the very radiant kings in the line of Vivasvan.
The one who properly recites this creation of Aditya Vivasvan, of the god Shraddhadeva, the giver of prosperity to creatures, becomes rich in offspring and attains union with Aditya Vivasvan.
There the remaining gods, the Tushitas, Brahmins, went to Brahma for refuge, the primal, eternal god.
Then, restraining Ushanas and Rudra Shankara, the Grandfather himself gave Tara to Angiras.
Seeing her pregnant, Brihaspati angrily said: "A child must not be borne by you in my womb at all."
Coming to a clump of reeds, she cast off the embryo; the child, as soon as born, outshone the gods' bodies with his radiance.
Then the foremost gods, falling into doubt, said to Tara: "Tell the truth: whose son is he, Soma's or Brihaspati's?"
When asked by the gods she did not answer them; then the boy, the best destroyer of enemies, began to curse her.
Brahma, restraining him, then asked Tara about the doubt: "Tell the truth in this matter, Tara: whose son is he?"
With joined palms she replied to the Grandfather, "Soma's." Then King Soma, kissing the son's head,
gave the intelligent boy the name Budha; and Budha rises in the sky in contrary fashion.
Then he begot a son on Vairaja's daughter; his offspring, very radiant, was Aila Pururavas.
On Urvashi he had seven great-souled sons. This birth of Soma has been told to you, increasing fame.
Hear, best of sages, his lineage as it is recited: blessed, life-giving, healthful, meritorious, accomplishing purposes.
By merely hearing the birth of Soma one is freed from sins.
Vishvayu, the righteous-souled, and Shrutayu, another; Dridhayu, Vanayu and Bahvayu were Urvashi's sons.
Amavasu's heir was King Bhima, a king of kings, glorious; Bhima's heir was the king Kanchanaprabha.
Kanchana's son, the learned Suhotra, was mighty; Suhotra had Jahnu, born from Keshini's womb,
who performed a great sacrificial session, the serpent sacrifice, a great rite; the Ganga, out of desire for a husband, approached him as husband.
Against his wish the Ganga flooded his sacrificial hall; seeing the sacrificial ground flooded all around by her,
the son of Suhotra, angry king, cursed the Ganga, Brahmins: "I make your effort fruitless by drinking up your waters.
Obtain at once, Ganga, the fruit of your arrogance." Seeing the Ganga drunk by the royal sage Jahnu, the great sages
brought the fortunate Jahnavi to him as his daughter. Jahnu married Kaveri, daughter of Yuvanashva.
By Yuvanashva's curse, Kaveri, best of rivers, came forth from half of the Ganga, the blameless wife of Jahnu.
Jahnu begot on Kaveri a beloved righteous son named Sunadya; his son was Ajaka.
Ajaka's heir was the king Balakashva, fond of hunting; Kusha was his son.
Kusha had four sons, radiant as gods: Kushika, Kushanabha, Kushamba and Murtiman.
The king, ever wandering in the forest, grew up with cowherds; Kushika performed austerity, desiring a son like Indra.
May I obtain one, he thought; Shakra, in fear, came and was born (as his son). When a full thousand years were complete, then Shakra saw,
seeing his exceedingly severe austerity, the thousand-eyed Purandara: though able himself to produce a son for him, eternal,
the chief of gods, best of the gods, arranged it for the sake of a son. He became Gadhi, the king, Maghavan Kaushika himself.
Paura was his wife; Gadhi was born of her. Gadhi had a fortunate, auspicious daughter named Satyavati.
The lord Gadhi gave her to Richika, son of Kavya, a Bhargava, the delight of Bhrigu's family; he was her pleased husband.
For the sake of a son he prepared a charu (oblation) for her and likewise one for Gadhi. Then Richika the Bhargava called his wife and said:

This charu is to be eaten by you, fair one, and the other by your mother; from you a radiant son, a bull among Kshatriyas, will be born,
brahmapuran:10:32	unconquerable by Kshatriyas in the world, a destroyer of the bulls among Kshatriyas. And for you too, auspicious one, this charu will bring a son, steadfast, rich in austerity,
brahmapuran:10:33	peaceful of nature, the best of Brahmins. Having said so to his wife, Richika the Bhargava
ever devoted to austerity, entered the forest. Gadhi with his wife then went to Richika's hermitage,
in the course of a pilgrimage, to see his daughter. Then Satyavati took the two charus from the sage,
and carefully told her mother. Her mother, by fate, gave her own charu to her daughter,
and through ignorance took her daughter's charu for herself. Then Satyavati bore the one destined to end the Kshatriyas,
with a radiant body, terrible to look upon. Richika, seeing her, approached her by yogic power,
and the best of Brahmins said to his lovely wife: "You were deceived by your mother, good one, through the exchange of the charus.
Your son will be cruel in deeds and exceedingly terrible; and your brother (nephew) will be born a Brahman-like ascetic.
For by austerity I placed all Brahman in him." Thus addressed by her husband, the fortunate Satyavati
appeased her husband: "May my son not be such." The sage, told "A Brahmin-disgrace comes from you," said:
This desire was not conceived by me, good one. So be it: the son will be of fierce deeds because of father and mother.
Again Satyavati said these words: "Sage, you can create even worlds, how much more a son!
You should give me a peaceful, upright son; let such a grandson be mine and yours, lord."
If it cannot be otherwise, best of Brahmins... then he showed favour to her by the strength of his austerity:
There is no difference to me between son and grandson, fair one; as you have said, so it shall be, good one.
Then Satyavati bore a Bhargava son, Jamadagni, devoted to austerity, self-controlled, peaceful of nature.
In this line of Bhrigu on earth Jamadagni was born. That Satyavati, meritorious and devoted to truth and dharma,
is called Kaushiki; this great river has come into being. Reņu, a king born of the Ikshvaku line,
had a fortunate daughter named Kamali, Renuka. On Renuka-Kamali, endowed with austerity and learning,
the son of Richika begot the very terrible Jamadagnya (Rama), versed in all sciences, best, master of the Dhanurveda,
Rama, destroyer of Kshatriyas, blazing like fire. Thus of Aurva's line Richika, on Satyavati, the greatly famed
Jamadagni was born by the power of austerity, the best of Brahman-knowers. The middle son was Shunahshepha, and the youngest Shunahpuchchha.
Gadhi, the delight of Kushika, begot an heir, Vishvamitra, a son peaceful through austerity and learning,
who, obtaining equality with Brahmin sages, attained the state of a Brahmin sage. The righteous-souled Vishvamitra is remembered by name as Vishvaratha.
By Bhrigu's favour he was born from Kaushika, increaser of the line. Vishvamitra's sons are remembered as Devarata and the others,
famed in the three worlds; their names follow: Devarata, Kati — from whom the Katyayanas are remembered —
Hiranyaksha, born of Shalavati, Renu, Renuka, Sankriti, Galava and the famed Mudgala,
Madhuchchhandas, Jaya, Devala and Ashtaka, Kachchhapa and Harita: these were Vishvamitra's sons.
Of those great-souled Kaushikas the famed gotras are: Panin, Babhru, Dhyanajapya,
Parthiva, Devarata, Shalankayana, Bashkala, Lohita, Yamaduta and Karushaka are remembered.
Best of sages, the connection of the Pauravas with the Brahmin sage Kaushika in this lineage, a union of Brahmin and Kshatriya, is renowned.
Among Vishvamitra's sons Shunahshepha is remembered as the eldest; that best of sages, a Bhargava, had attained Kaushika status.
